A *deep compartment model* (DCM) keeps the structure of a classical pharmacokinetic
model, a system of ODEs describing how a drug moves through the body, but lets a
neural network predict the ODE parameters (clearance, volume, ...) from patient
covariates. This tutorial walks through the whole loop on a small, classical dataset:

1. build `Individual`s and a `Population` from a table,
2. define the neural network and the model,
3. fit it by minimising the sum of squared errors,
4. look at the predictions.

The data are the theophylline dataset: 12 subjects who each got a single oral dose and
were sampled over 24 hours. The only covariate is body weight.

## Setup

```{julia}
using DeepCompartmentModels   # also re-exports Lux, Optimisers, OrdinaryDiffEq, ...
using DataFrames, CSV
using CairoMakie
using Random
```

## Data

```{julia}
df = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "data", "theophylline.csv")))
first(df, 4)
```

Each subject has one dosing row (`DV` is `missing`) and a series of concentration
measurements. `AMT` is the dose in mg/kg, so the dose in mg is `AMT * WEIGHT`.

An `Individual` bundles the covariates `x`, the observation times `t`, the
observations `y` and a *dosing callback* that tells the ODE solver when and how much
drug enters the system. `generate_dosing_callback` builds that callback from a matrix
with one row per dose, `[time amount]`:

```{julia}
function make_individual(g)
    obs = g[.!ismissing.(g.DV), :]
    dose = g.AMT[1] * g.WEIGHT[1]                      # mg
    callback = generate_dosing_callback([0.0 dose])    # a bolus at t = 0
    return Individual(g.ID[1], [g.WEIGHT[1]], obs.TIME, obs.DV, callback)
end

population = Population([make_individual(g) for g in groupby(df, :ID)])
length(population), population[1]
```

Everything is stored as `Float32` by default. A `Population` behaves like a vector of
individuals, so it can be indexed and sliced; `get_t`, `get_y` and `get_x` pull out the
times, observations and covariates.

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (700, 350))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Time (h)", ylabel = "Concentration (mg/L)")
for indv in population
    scatterlines!(ax, get_t(indv), get_y(indv); color = (:steelblue, 0.6), markersize = 7)
end
fig
```

## The model

Theophylline is absorbed from the gut and eliminated from the central compartment, so
we use `one_comp_abs!`, a built-in ODE with a depot and a central compartment. Its
parameters are `[kₐ, CL, V]`: the absorption rate, the clearance and the volume of
distribution. The package ships `one_comp!`, `one_comp_abs!`, `two_comp!` and
`two_comp_abs!`; the [custom ODE tutorial](06-custom-ode.md) shows how to write your own.

The network maps the (normalised) weight to those three positive parameters:

```{julia}
ann = Lux.Chain(
    Normalize([100f0]),                  # min-max scale weight with an upper bound of 100 kg
    Lux.Dense(1, 8, tanh),
    Lux.Dense(8, 3, Lux.softplus),       # kₐ, CL and V must be positive
    Lux.WrappedFunction(x -> x .* Float32[1, 3, 30]),  # start near plausible magnitudes
)
```

The last layer rescales the outputs so that training starts at physiologically
plausible values (a volume of about 30 L rather than 1 L). This is a modelling choice,
not a requirement.

```{julia}
problem = ODEProblem(one_comp_abs!, zeros(Float32, 2), (-0.1f0, 1f0); dt = 0.01f0)
model = DCM(problem, ann; target = 2)
```

The time span of the problem is a placeholder: it is replaced by the span of each
individual when solving. Its *start* matters, though. It has to lie before the first
dose, because the dosing callback only fires at times the solver steps to after
starting. Hence `-0.1`, which is also what `DCM(ode_fn, ...)` uses.

`target = 2` selects which ODE state is compared to the observations. In
`one_comp_abs!` state 1 is the *amount* in the depot and state 2 the *concentration*
in the central compartment, which is what was measured. (The default is `target = 1`.)

::: {.callout-tip}
`DCM(one_comp_abs!, ann)` builds the `ODEProblem` for you. Creating it explicitly, as
here, lets you pass solver defaults along: the `dt = 0.01f0` is the solver's *initial*
step size. Every individual starts with an empty body, and the solver's automatic
choice of a first step then logs a "dt_epsilon" warning on each of the thousands of
solves in a fit. The initial `dt` is only a starting point, the step size is still
adaptive. The same keyword (and `reltol`, `abstol`, `solver`, ...) can also be passed to
`predict`.
:::

## Fitting

`setup` initialises the parameters `ps` (what is learned) and the state `st`
(constants of the model) for a given objective. `SSE()` is the sum of squared errors:

```{julia}
rng = Random.Xoshiro(1)
objective = SSE()
ps, st = setup(objective, rng, model)
objective(model, population, ps, st)
```

Objectives are plain callables, `objective(model, data, ps, st)`. `gradient`
returns the gradient of the objective with respect to `ps`, with the same structure as
`ps`, so it plugs straight into [Optimisers.jl](https://github.com/FluxML/Optimisers.jl):

```{julia}
function train(objective, model, population, ps, st; epochs, lr)
    opt_state = Optimisers.setup(Optimisers.Adam(lr), ps)
    losses = Float32[]
    for _ in 1:epochs
        ∇ = gradient(objective, model, population, ps, st)
        opt_state, ps = Optimisers.update(opt_state, ps, ∇)
        push!(losses, objective(model, population, ps, st))
    end
    return ps, losses
end

ps, losses = train(objective, model, population, ps, st; epochs = 150, lr = 0.02f0)
losses[[1, 50, 100, 150]]
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
# Seeded check, so that the docs build fails if the model stops learning
@assert last(losses) < 0.6 * first(losses) "SSE only went from $(first(losses)) to $(last(losses))"
@assert last(losses) < 350 "final SSE $(last(losses)) is far above the usual ≈230"
```

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (500, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Epoch", ylabel = "Sum of squared errors", yscale = log10)
lines!(ax, losses)
fig
```

## Predictions

`predict(model, data, ps, st)` solves the ODE for every individual and returns the
predicted observations at the observed times. Pass `saveat` for a dense grid:

```{julia}
ŷ = predict(model, population, ps, st)
ŷ[1]
```

```{julia}
grid = 0:0.25:24
fig = Figure(size = (900, 600))
for (i, indv) in enumerate(population)
    local ax = Axis(fig[fld(i - 1, 4) + 1, mod1(i, 4)]; title = "ID $(indv.id)",
              xlabel = i > 8 ? "Time (h)" : "", ylabel = mod1(i, 4) == 1 ? "mg/L" : "")
    lines!(ax, grid, predict(model, indv, ps, st; saveat = grid); color = :firebrick)
    scatter!(ax, get_t(indv), get_y(indv); color = :black, markersize = 6)
end
fig
```

The network has learned a weight-dependent set of parameters. `predict_typ_parameters`
returns them for any set of individuals, one column per individual:

```{julia}
ζ, _ = predict_typ_parameters(model, population, ps, st)
DataFrame(permutedims(ζ), ["ka (1/h)", "CL (L/h)", "V (L)"])
```

::: {.callout-note}
With only 12 subjects and one covariate this is a demonstration of the mechanics, not
a serious model: there is no way to tell here whether the weight effect is real. The
next tutorials add inter-individual variability and a likelihood.
:::
